thought.text: Now I have the full picture. Let me reproduce the QGIS command failure to confirm the root cause (the folded heredoc):

reasoning_content:
Now all the issues are clear:

**Issue A — nginx (dev compose bug):** `docker-compose.dev.yml` mounts `./nginx/nginx.conf` (a full main config with `worker_processes`) to `/etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf`, where a `server` block is expected. The official nginx image then fails: `"worker_processes" directive is not allowed here`. The production compose correctly mounts `nginx.conf` to `/etc/nginx/nginx.conf` and `default.conf` to `conf.d/default.conf`. So the dev compose nginx mount is wrong.

Fix: in `docker-compose.dev.yml`, change the nginx volume to `- ./nginx/nginx.conf:/etc/nginx/nginx.conf:ro` (keeping the main config's include of conf.d/*, and the image's default site at /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf will be included — wait, the official nginx image ships a default.conf at conf.d/. That defines a server on port 80 and serves static html. The repo's nginx.conf includes /etc/nginx/conf.d/*.conf. If we mount only nginx.conf, the image's default default.conf will be active, and the repo's default.conf will not be. That changes routing (API requests won't be proxied to backend).

Better dev fix: mount both like the prod compose:
- ./nginx/nginx.conf:/etc/nginx/nginx.conf:ro
- ./nginx/default.conf:/etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf:ro
This matches the prod pattern exactly and makes the repo's routing config active (it overrides the image default with the same path).

But wait — there's a subtle point: default.conf references `upstream backend_wms { server backend-wms:8000; }`. There is no backend-wms service in the dev compose. nginx only resolves upstream hostnames at startup for nameservers-based resolution… no wait — actually, nginx resolves `server` directives inside upstream blocks from DNS at config load time. If the `backend-wms` host doesn't exist on the docker network, nginx will fail with "host not found in upstream backend-wms".

Hmm, so in dev mode the upstream backend_wms can't resolve → nginx fails to start. Let me confirm: does the nginx config need variables? In default.conf: `upstream backend_wms { server backend-wms:8000; }` — static name → resolved at startup → will fail if no such container exists.

So, to make nginx work in dev, the dev compose either needs to also include the backend-wms service (as prod does), or default.conf needs to reference only backend. The dev Caddyfile routes the api.localhost and admin.localhost panels to nginx:80, and also uses forward_auth nginx:80 for qgis/files. The api.localhost proxy → nginx → default.conf location / → proxy_pass http://backend. The wms-proxy location references backend_wms.

Simplest, consistent dev fix: add the `backend-wms` service to the dev compose (a copy of prod's backend-wms but sized smaller) — this is the same image (qonnectra/backend:dev already built). This gives full parity with prod (the WMS proxy works in dev too).

Alternative: remove the upstream backend_wms and its location from default.conf. But default.conf is shared with prod (where backend-wms exists). Modifying the shared config risks breaking prod. Adding a service to the dev compose is less invasive.

Also, in the dev compose the nginx.conf includes `proxy_cache_path /var/cache/nginx/wms` and `mvt_cache` — the dev nginx service doesn't declare a wms_cache volume, but that's fine, it'll be written to the container's writable layer.

Wait, one more check on nginx.conf: it mounts to /etc/nginx/nginx.conf in prod. In prod it includes /etc/nginx/conf.d/*.conf — and prod mounts default.conf there. The image's own default.conf is at /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf, so prod's mount overrides it. In dev, if we mount default.conf to the same path, it will also override.

**Issue B — tileserver:** `Not valid input file: "/data/germany.mbtiles"` → exit(1). The README explicitly documents that mbtiles must be generated by the user (Planetiler, requires Java 17+, downloads OSM Germany data — huge). The container "restarts" in a loop, but tileserver is not part of the core app's dependencies (it's just the basemap layer). Hmm — is this an "installation failure"? The guide (Quick Start) lists TileServer as one of the access points. Deployment README section 2.2 just says `docker compose up -d --build` — it doesn't repeat the mbtiles prerequisite in the dev flow (it's in the services overview / troubleshooting).

Options:
1. Leave tileserver failing (documented optional component, user data).
2. Try to generate a minimal valid mbtiles so tileserver can at least start. Planetiler needs Java and multi-GB of OSM data — heavy, but there's a `--area=berlin` option (smaller). Still, it downloads OSM PBF (a few hundred MB) and takes 10+ minutes. Java isn't installed; apt-get install openjdk-17 — is that possible in this container? The host is Debian-based (has apt? let me check). Actually, this adds a lot of time and might still fail (the 8GB -Xmx suggestion vs 7.6GB of RAM).

A lighter option: create a minimal valid mbtiles file (SQLite with proper schema) so tileserver can start and serve an empty vector layer. TileServer-GL's "Not valid input file" check requires a valid SQLite DB with an mbtiles schema (metadata, tiles tables). A minimal empty mbtiles is a few KB and makes tileserver fully functional (just no map data — matches the state of "user-generated data not yet provided"). But is that a legitimate "installation"? TileServer's job per the README: "Generate mbtiles using Planetiler before starting TileServer (setup required)". So the documented setup requires user-generated data; providing a placeholder empty mbtiles is a deviation, but it lets the service start. Hmm.

Actually, wait — I should reconsider: can I really not get the real germany.mbtiles? Planetiler needs: Java 17+, ~8GB RAM, download OSM Germany extract (~2.5GB? no — germany-latest.osm.pbf is around 500MB–1GB; actually the German PBF extract is around 450MB). On 8GB RAM with -Xmx4g it might work (Planetiler can run on 4GB for a country). That's a big time investment (10–30 min). Per the README it's a documented setup requirement, but it's described as a user data step ("you need to generate mbtiles before starting TileServer"), not part of the core installation. The Quick Start access point list includes TileServer.

Let me think about what "installing the assigned software" means: Qonnectra — a fiber-optic documentation app for passive networks. Core software = backend (API + admin), frontend, database, QGIS server. TileServer is an optional basemap layer ("Setup Required: Generate mbtiles..."). The deployment README marks this as a setup requirement for that component.

Decision: first try the lightweight path — create a minimal valid mbtiles so tileserver starts and serves the light/dark styles (with no tiles in the data). No actually…hmm, wait. Let me reconsider. Does tileserver-gl exit(1) when the input file is invalid, or does it just warn? From the logs: "Not valid input file" then "Starting tileserver-gl" "Starting server" "Listening at ..." — and then it's back to restarting in a loop. So it's exiting after binding. Yes, it's exiting.

Actually, let me look at the tileserver-gl source behavior: in v5, `initData` catches invalid input files: logs "Not valid input file" and calls `process.exit(1)`. Yeah.

Minimal mbtiles: SQLite DB with `tiles` table (z,x,y,id? v3 schema: tiles(zoom_level, tile_column, tile_row, tile_data) and metadata table). Let me create it with the sqlite3 CLI… is sqlite3 on the host? The host doesn't have python3… maybe it has the sqlite3 binary. Or create it inside a container: I can use the postgis image (it has psql, sqlite3? probably not). The backend image is python:3.12-slim — python has the sqlite3 module built in! I can create the mbtiles using `docker run --rm -v ... qonnectra/backend:dev python ...`.

But wait — should I? An empty placeholder mbtiles deviates from the documented setup (user-generated Planetiler data). It's a reasonable "make the service startable" workaround that I'd have to disclose in additional_actions. Given the goal is "install the software and verify it works", it's better to have tileserver running with an empty overlay than crash-looping, I think. And I'll clearly document it.

Hmm, actually, hold on. Let me reconsider the scope. Rule: "Treat the provided installation guide as the primary source of installation instructions." The guide's Quick Start = .env + docker compose up. Deployment README = details. TileServer data generation is explicitly documented as a user task ("Setup Required"). I'll do the minimal placeholder to let the stack come up fully, and note it.

Alternatively, I could try Planetiler properly — check if Java is available/installable. Let me at least check whether the host has java. If java is easily available, I could try `--area=germany` with -Xmx4g… but OSM download (500MB+) + build (5–15 min on 8 cores). It would be the "correct" data. But risk: 7.6GB RAM — 4GB for planetiler + OS + docker image build cache… might work. But time budget is a concern (600s per command; a build could take 10–30 min in the background).

Let me try Planetiler as the documented approach in the background, and prepare a placeholder mbtiles as a fallback. Actually… let me first check if java is available.

**Issue C — QGIS:** exit code 0, log 0 lines, restarts every ~20 seconds. The command chain ends in `tail -f /dev/null` (infinite) — for it to exit with code 0 before reaching tail, one of the earlier `&&` steps must have exited with 0 without starting tail. Candidates: `grep -q 'client_max_body_size' /etc/nginx/nginx.conf` — if it matches, grep exits with 0, `sed` is skipped, chain continues to `nginx &&` — nginx (foreground daemon mode!) — the `nginx` binary by default runs as a daemon (master process forks to background) and exits 0 immediately! Then `spawn-fcgi ... &&` runs, and then `tail -f /dev/null` should hang forever…

Wait, so why is the container exiting? Unless spawn-fcgi failed… but then the exit code should be nonzero. Unless the whole `sh -c` was killed? Let me think — actually, `nginx` daemonizes: the master process forks to background and the foreground exits with 0. That's fine, the chain continues to spawn-fcgi. If spawn-fcgi succeeds, tail -f runs forever → container stays Up. But it's exiting with code 0…

Hmm wait, looking at the rendered command: `nginx && spawn-fcgi -F 2 ... && tail -f /dev/null`. But the log has 0 lines — not even output from Xvfb/fc-cache. Strange. If the sh process died instantly… could the container have been OOM-killed? OOMKilled=false.

Actually — wait a sec. Look at the restart timing: StartedAt 17:28:47.726, FinishedAt 17:28:47.936 — died 210ms after start, exit 0. And no logs at all. The first command is `mkdir -p /etc/postgresql-common` — instant. Then cat heredoc — instant. Xvfb — instant…

Hmm, actually, I bet the issue is the heredoc `<<EOF` inside the rendered sh -c string. In the rendered command: `cat > /etc/postgresql-common/pg_service.conf <<EOF\n[qonnectra] host=db ... sslmode=disable EOF\n  mkdir...` — the heredoc terminator `EOF` needs to be at the start of the line (unquoted <<EOF, no leading whitespace allowed). In the rendered string, is `EOF` at the start of the line? Looking at the rendering: `...disable EOF\n  mkdir` — there's a space before "mkdir", but is "EOF" alone on its own line? The JSON shows: `host=db port=5432 dbname=qonnectra user=qgis_user password=... sslmode=disable EOF\n` — so the line containing EOF is `[qonnectra] host=db ... sslmode=disable EOF` — the heredoc terminator isn't alone on its own line, it's appended at the end of the config line! With `<<EOF` (unquoted, non-`<<-`), the terminator must be exactly `EOF` at the start of a line. So the heredoc never terminates… sh waits for the terminator at the end of the script → treats the rest of the command as heredoc content → heredoc never terminates → but that should hang, not exit with 0…

Hmm, actually, in a non-interactive `sh -c`, an unterminated heredoc at end-of-input: does dash print an error? Let me think: dash gives "sh: 1: Syntax error: EOF in heredoc" or something similar? In dash: unbounded heredoc at EOF → "sh: 2: Syntax error: EOF in heredoc" with exit code 2. But the exit code is 0!

Wait, maybe the rendered output from docker inspect isn't showing all the newlines. Let me get the raw command with proper formatting. Actually, the inspect output is JSON-escaped: `...<<EOF\n[qonnectra] host=db port=5432 dbname=qonnectra user=qgis_user password=6a91c3e04b5278fd1c23b4a8e0d917c5 sslmode=disable EOF\n  mkdir -p...`. Hmm, so the heredoc content line is `[qonnectra] host=db ... sslmode=disable EOF` — all on one line. The original YAML (dev compose) is:

```
      cat > /etc/postgresql-common/pg_service.conf <<EOF
    [${QGIS_PG_SERVICE_NAME:-qonnectra}]
    host=db
    ...
    EOF
```

YAML block scalar `>` folds newlines into spaces! The `command: >` folding collapses each line into a single line separated by spaces. That's why in the rendered string `[qonnectra]` host=db ... sslmode=disable EOF are all on one line. So the heredoc terminator `EOF` never appears alone at the start of a line → sh -c receives a script with an unterminated heredoc → dash: at EOF, dash prints an error like "dash: 1: Syntax error: EOF in heredoc"? Let me actually test what dash does with an unterminated heredoc: `echo test | dash -c 'cat <<EOF\nhello'` → dash: 1: Syntax error: EOF in heredoc, exit code 2. But we're seeing exit code 0…

Hmm wait, actually maybe not. Let me re-read: `<<EOF` — for the heredoc to work, the terminator line must be exactly `EOF`. After folding, the script is:

```
sh -c "
  mkdir -p /etc/postgresql-common &&
  cat > /etc/postgresql-common/pg_service.conf <<EOF
[qonnectra] host=db port=5432 dbname=qonnectra user=qgis_user password=... sslmode=disable EOF
  mkdir -p /var/www/data/qgis &&
  ... rest ...
  tail -f /dev/null
"
```

The first line `mkdir ... &&` — sh parses the first line: `mkdir -p /etc/postgresql-common &&` — wait, the `&&` at the end of the first line is a continuation: sh reads the next line to complete the command: `cat > file <<EOF` — and then the heredoc body starts from the next line: everything from `[qonnectra]...` to the end of the script is heredoc body (since EOF is never alone on a line) → end of input → syntax error "EOF in heredoc" (dash) with non-zero exit.

But the exit code is 0! So maybe sh (the QGIS image is Ubuntu noble → /bin/sh = dash). Let me actually test it: does dash exit with 2? Let me reproduce exactly in the qgis image:

docker run --rm qgis/qgis-server:3.44.7-noble sh -c '<the exact folded string>' ; echo $?

That'll tell us. Actually, more directly: the container's exit code is 0 and no logs… whatever the mechanism, empirically the command is failing. The folded heredoc is almost certainly the culprit: the pg_service.conf isn't being written correctly, and the script is erroring out.

Wait, actually — if it's a syntax error, the exit code should be 2 and there should be an error message in the log. Log is empty (0 lines), exit 0. Confusing!

Let me look again… ah, wait. I think the problem is somewhere else. Let me look at the rendered command one more time:

`"sh","-c","\n  mkdir -p /etc/postgresql-common &&\n  cat > /etc/postgresql-common/pg_service.conf <<EOF\n[qonnectra] host=db port=5432 dbname=qonnectra user=qgis_user password=6a91c3e04b5278fd1c23b4a8e0d917c5 sslmode=disable EOF\n  mkdir -p /var/www/data/qgis &&\n..."`

Hmm — with an unterminated heredoc at end of input, dash actually… let me just test it. I'll run it in the image.

Actually — I recall dash's behavior: `sh -c 'cat <<EOF'` (unterminated heredoc at end of input) → dash: no output, exit code 2? Let me test empirically in the container.

Whatever the exact mechanism, the dev compose `command: >` folding breaks the heredoc — this is a dev compose bug (the prod compose uses a `command:` list with a proper multi-line string, preserving newlines: the prod compose uses a `command: - sh - -c - |` list → the `|` literal block scalar preserves newlines → the heredoc works). So prod is fine, dev is broken.

Fix options for dev:
1. Change the dev compose to use the same list-form command as prod (`- sh`, `- -c`, `- |` literal block) to preserve newlines.
2. Avoid the heredoc: replace with printf (single line, folding-safe).

Option 2 is less invasive to the YAML structure:
```
printf '[%s]\nhost=db\nport=5432\ndbname=%s\nuser=%s\npassword=%s\nsslmode=disable\n' "$${QGIS_PG_SERVICE_NAME}" "$${DB_NAME}" "$${QGIS_DB_USER}" "$${QGIS_DB_PASSWORD}" > /etc/postgresql-common/pg_service.conf
```
(prod uses exactly this printf approach! And the prod compose has the same heredoc issue? no — prod uses a literal `|` block so the heredoc isn't in there. Prod uses printf. Yes, prod's command uses printf.)

So the dev compose heredoc approach was a regression; switching to printf (like prod) is a clean, minimal fix that preserves the folded single-line command.

But wait — I should confirm the actual failure first. Let me reproduce the qgis command failure inside a one-off container and get the real error.

Also, the nginx.conf sed: `grep -q 'client_max_body_size' /etc/nginx/nginx.conf || sed ...` — the qgis image's /etc/nginx/nginx.conf is the standard one; the grep fails → sed adds a line after `http {`. Fine.

And `nginx` daemonizes OK; `spawn-fcgi` requires /var/lib/qgis to exist (it does in the image). OK.

So the qgis fix = printf. Let me first verify the actual failure mode.

Now — one more consideration for the nginx dev fix: I need to add the `backend-wms` service to the dev compose because default.conf has `upstream backend_wms`. Otherwise nginx will fail to start ("host not found in upstream"). Let me double-check the dev Caddyfile: it's the same Caddyfile (tls internal) — routes api.localhost → nginx:80, admin.localhost → nginx:80, qgis.localhost forward_auth nginx:80 + proxy qgis-server:80, app.localhost → frontend:3000, files.localhost forward_auth + webdav, tiles.localhost → tileserver:8080.

So in dev, the API goes through nginx. nginx needs to start. With only the nginx.conf mounted (my proposed fix) + default.conf mounted + no backend-wms service → upstream resolution fails → nginx dies. So add a backend-wms service (same image) to the dev compose. That's the minimal, parity-preserving fix.

Alright, let me now verify the qgis failure mode precisely, then apply the three fixes:

1. dev compose nginx volume: mount nginx.conf→/etc/nginx/nginx.conf, default.conf→conf.d/default.conf (+ add wms_cache volume? nginx.conf's proxy_cache_path writes to /var/cache/nginx/wms — in dev the container layer is enough; but to be closer to prod, I could add the wms_cache volume… let me keep it minimal: don't add the volume; cache is ephemeral in dev. Hmm, actually the wms_cache named volume in prod avoids the cache being lost on restart. In dev the container layer is enough.)

2. Add backend-wms service to dev compose (sized smaller than prod, dev naming: qonnectra_backend_wms_dev, no wms_cache volume mount… wait, the backend-wms command is just gunicorn, the volume is static/media. No problem.)

3. qgis-server command: replace heredoc with printf.

4. tileserver: create a minimal valid mbtiles placeholder (disclose it), or try Planetiler. Let me check if java is present.

Then restart and verify all endpoints.

Now let me test the qgis command failure in a one-off container.

action.command:
docker run --rm qgis/qgis-server:3.44.7-noble sh -c 'printf "test: "; sh -c "
  echo line1 &&
  cat > /tmp/out.txt <<EOF
[a] host=db port=5432 dbname=qonnectra user=qgis_user password=x sslmode=disable EOF
  echo line2
"; echo "exit=$?"; cat /tmp/out.txt 2>&1' 2>&1
